sections.heading: One platform for every robot the lab owns
sections.body: agentAI is a research-data platform for physical and embodied agents, built at the MTSU Great Robotics Lab. A robot, a drone or a sensor rig is a project. A project owns its keys, its people and a locked dataset registry. Agents on the platform harvest, filter, label and train against that registry. Adding a robot is a configuration, not a migration.

sections.heading: Any research field is a project
sections.body: A lab member opens a project for any data type and any field, uploads images, video or sensor logs, and gets an automatic diagnosis before choosing what to do next. Weed detection is one project on this platform. So are the 241 rover and the laser cart, and so is a humanoid project that is open and still empty.

sections.heading: Inside the platform
sections.body: Every stage from a camera in a crop row to a checkpoint on the cluster has run. The dashboard and registry run on a lab server; GPU jobs queue on PSC Bridges-2. The collector and trainer are paused after a stop-loss on 2026-08-29. The supervisor is advisory and nothing it says is applied.

sections.heading: Robots on the platform today
sections.body: Robot 241 is a tracked rover that drives crop rows and streams camera, GPS and two IMUs. The laser cart carries the weeder: a galvanometer laser, a down camera over the work zone and a forward camera. Ten projects sit on the platform and two of them have a robot reporting into them. Between those two vehicles, 2,686 frames in 26 drives.

sections.heading: Four frames, as recorded
sections.body: Nothing here is enhanced and nothing is labelled. The rectangle in the cart's down camera is a fixed work-zone overlay: it sits at the same pixels on frames with no vegetation in them at all.

sections.heading: Frames from both vehicles
sections.body: Four frames off the archive, unenhanced and unlabelled, from the two vehicles that drive our own crop plots.

sections.heading: Adding the next robot
sections.body: A new robot needs a project, an API key and a session start. The ingest contract is the same for every vehicle: open a session, post sensor batches and frames while driving, stop. The platform does not care what the robot is. Empty projects for a mobile robot and a humanoid already sit on it, waiting for a first upload.

sections.heading: A drive becomes a dataset as it opens
sections.body: A vehicle opens a session and the platform registers it as a governed dataset at that moment, not after the drive ends. Frames and sensor batches arrive over one API key. Robot 241 sends camera, GPS and two IMUs; the laser cart sends camera, laser state, vehicle telemetry and its own detections, and no position at all.

sections.heading: On disk today
sections.body: Two robots have put 2,686 camera frames and 91,955 telemetry rows across nine streams onto the platform, over 26 drives, with 342 m of GPS track from 1,502 fixes. None of the frames is labelled.

sections.heading: 213 seconds in one crop plot
sections.body: The longest single pass the platform holds: 141 m of track from 211 fixes, with heading from the IMU over the same 213 seconds. The platform holds 18 passes that carry position.

sections.heading: Every drive is diagnosed on arrival
sections.body: The platform runs a fixed diagnosis over each finished session without being asked: route, noise, cross-sensor correlation, a timeline. It has done that for 26 live robot sessions and written 45 charts. A person reads the diagnosis before deciding whether the drive is worth anything.
sections.big_label: live drives diagnosed without being asked

sections.heading: Driving a robot from a browser
sections.body: A signed-in user opens the 241 project and clicks Drive. The platform reverse-proxies the robot's own console over the lab tailnet, so the rover is driven from a plain browser with no VPN client. 1,389 joystick commands have gone through that path. Two gates sit in front of it: the platform's Google login, then the robot's own password.

sections.heading: Only one robot has the button
sections.body: The Drive button appears on the 241 project and not on the laser cart's, because the allow-list holds one target. The rover has been dark since 2026-08-28: the platform answers a drive request today with its own offline page. The cart has never been drivable from the platform.

sections.heading: Talking back to a robot
sections.body: Besides the drive relay, the platform sends a robot exactly one thing: advisory text. The rover polls for it and shows deterministic warnings about battery, current and temperature. That poll has returned 406 times. No platform code path sends an actuation command to any robot.

sections.heading: Laser on, never once at a target
sections.body: The cart's own operator switched the laser on during three of eight archived sessions. The platform recorded 3379 laser rows and 216 of them have the laser enabled. Every one of those 216 is in OBSERVATION phase, with no target. The laser has never been armed, aimed or fired by the platform.
sections.big_label: times the laser has been fired by the platform

sections.heading: Ask a dataset what it is good for
sections.body: Every dataset page carries a chat box. A user types or speaks a plain question about that dataset. A planner reads the question and the dataset's real column profile, then picks from 14 fixed analysis tools or writes new code. The answer comes back with the chart and the code that produced it.
sections.big_label: analysis tools the planner can choose from

sections.heading: Asked something it had never seen
sections.body: Asked to plot a histogram of the heading change rate on the 241 field drive, the agent wrote the code and returned the plot on the first attempt. A fixed template cannot do that, because nothing in the platform knew that question would be asked. Across the platform, 9 datasets carry 92 turns of that conversation.
sections.big_label: questions asked of a dataset so far

sections.heading: Code the agent writes runs fenced in
sections.body: Generated code passes an import whitelist and an AST check before it runs, with no network and no file writes, 15 seconds of CPU, 1.5 GB of memory and a 25 second wall clock. A user can edit the agent's code or paste their own and re-run it in the same fence.

sections.heading: Not yet pointed at the drives
sections.body: The conversational agent has answered 92 questions, and none of them was about a live robot drive. Every one of the 26 live sessions got the fixed diagnosis; not one got a question. Pointing the agent at the drives is the next thing to do and it costs nothing but asking.

sections.heading: Left alone for fifteen rounds
sections.body: Two cluster jobs, one collecting and one training, ran fifteen rounds against the locked registry with nobody in the room. Each round searched public sources, filtered what it found, merged, trained and evaluated. Every round reported success. Accuracy fell for fifteen rounds.

sections.heading: Which decisions a model makes
sections.body: A language model decides what the collector goes after next, judges whether a candidate dataset is on topic, and reviews a finished step. Those run on the cluster, as batch jobs, on open weights. The lab box hosts only the small guide model, and a verdict produced there is marked in its own record as a draft that may not be reported.

sections.heading: Who notices when it breaks
sections.body: We froze 162 real failures out of this project's own engineering record and scored every kind of supervision against them. The watchdog the loop was running returned no decision on any of the 149 dev cases. A model reading the raw artifacts reaches 0.70 recall over 116 incidents.
sections.big_label: real failures frozen as a benchmark

sections.heading: Grounded recall separates the reviewers
sections.body: A 7 B model has the highest recall on the page and two thirds of what it reports quotes a line that does not exist. The 27 B leaves no such gap. The retrieval tier is worth +0.149 recall to the 27 B and +0.012 to the 14 B, so tiering pays where the model can use it.

sections.heading: Reading the loop's own artifacts
sections.body: The corpus stopped growing at round three: the same 24 datasets and 48,752 unique images went in every time, and the apparent growth was one staging directory nobody cleared. Eight rounds collected nothing and reported success. Starting fresh instead of from the previous round's weights is worth +0.0287, 5.1 times this recipe's own seed spread.

sections.heading: Six months, in order
sections.body: Four of these eight turns are things that did not work, and two are numbers this project measured and then withdrew after checking them.

sections.heading: Everything we trained, ran, or rejected
sections.body: Thirty rows in four families, which is 27 distinct models. Five detectors trained on our own holdout, two vision models inside the loop, fourteen vision-language models zero-shot, and nine language models as reviewers. One is deployed.
sections.big_label: distinct models trained, run, or rejected

sections.heading: More web data, less accuracy
sections.body: Twelve times the training data costs 0.0189 on our own 1,977-image holdout, three seeds at every rung, which is 8.2 times the seed spread. The same eight checkpoints fall on a second weed dataset too. One of six audited web sources reaches a 0.90 label-precision bar.

sections.heading: Back on our own rows
sections.body: The deployable checkpoint draws a box on 25 of the 2,686 frames our robots recorded, and 24 of those 25 boxes are the same class. These frames carry no labels, so that is a firing rate, not recall and not precision.

sections.heading: Auditing six web sources
sections.body: The same probe reads 1.000 on human-labelled CottonWeedDet12, so a source at 0.184 is the data and not the instrument. Only the top source clears the bar, and it supplies 3,208 of the 13,527 audited images.

sections.heading: Standing today
sections.body: The collector and trainer are paused after a stop-loss on 2026-08-29. The rover has been off the tailnet since then and the platform answers a drive request with its offline page. The supervisor is advisory. None of the 2,686 frames is labelled.

sections.heading: How the numbers were made
sections.body: Most in-domain numbers are mAP50-95 on the same 1,977 images under Ultralytics. RF-DETR is pycocotools and the zero-shot column is mAP50 on the 848-image split; neither is differenced against the rest. That holdout is also the validation set during training, so every mAP here is a run's best epoch.

sections.heading: Numbers we withdrew
sections.body: 0.910 was a data leak, found by a content-level check we built after publishing it. 0.9033 is the best of four unseeded runs and only one of the four crossed 0.90. An earlier reading of the ladder as a flat curve is retracted.

sections.heading: Size of the thing
sections.body: One FastAPI service on a lab server carries 151 routes in its main module plus more in mounted modules. 29 people sign in with a Google account, under two roles, with a per-user grant for cluster GPU. 10 projects sit on it and two of them have a robot reporting into them.
sections.big_label: projects, two of them with a robot on the other end

sections.heading: Building an agent by saying what you want
sections.body: A member types one sentence on the home page, or speaks it. A model proposes a project name, a modality and a set of agent components, the member edits what it got wrong, and the project exists. Speech goes through a Whisper model hosted on the lab's own GPU, not a cloud service.

sections.heading: Running the detector on a live frame
sections.body: While a robot is driving, the project page shows its newest frame refreshing every second and a half, and the weed detector can be switched on over that frame in the same process. The operator sees what the model sees, on the drive that is happening.

sections.heading: Rates the platform holds
sections.body: Robot 241 samples its two IMUs, its telemetry and its control stream at 20 Hz and its GPS at 1 Hz, and sends camera frames at one per second. The laser cart streams its own detections and laser state at 5 Hz and vehicle state at 2 Hz. Telemetry travels as one gzip batch per second with a sequence number, and the platform dedupes on it.

sections.heading: Where a human labels
sections.body: A member pushes a dataset's images to one of four allow-listed Roboflow projects under a per-project image budget, labels there, and pulls the labels back into the registry. Mongo holds the registry and is the source of truth; Roboflow is the labelling surface and nothing else.

sections.heading: Bugs this platform found in itself
sections.body: Until 2026-09-11 every derived GPS file on the platform was one motionless point, because the materialiser preferred the Pi's frozen fix over the board's. Reading the artifacts rather than the dashboard is what surfaced it, and 200.9 m of real track came back.

sections.heading: Any robot the lab owns joins the same platform
sections.body: Each of the four was opened the same way, sends through the same ingest contract, and is trained and evaluated by the same agents. Three have data. The fourth is open and empty, which is what a platform looks like before the next robot arrives.

sections.heading: One robot's model on another robot's rows
sections.body: Because every vehicle writes into one registry through one contract, a model trained on one robot's frames can be evaluated on another's without any new plumbing: the split is a query. We have run that query across datasets rather than across robots, and it is the hard direction. A detector trained on 40,000 harvested images loses 0.0299 on a second weed dataset; the same eight checkpoints fall on both exams. So sharing perception between the rover, the cart and whatever comes next is a measurement problem we have already priced, not a wiring problem.

sections.heading: How many agents, and which models
sections.body: Nothing on the platform hard-codes a model name. A router maps a role -- collector, judge, reviewer, planner -- onto a model and a place, and the place decides whether the verdict counts: work that analyses, reviews or decides runs as a cluster batch job on open weights, and anything answered by the lab box is marked in its own record as a draft. The scheduler then fans a round out across as many review arms as the round asks for. What it does not yet do is choose that number for itself.

sections.heading: Where this goes
sections.body: The end state is one general platform: any dataset, any research field, any robot. Agents on it run without being asked, iterate on their own output, escalate to a larger model when they are out of their depth, and are fenced in a sandbox while they do it. Every piece of this poster is a step in that direction rather than a one-off experiment.

sections.heading: Why it is built this way
sections.body: Each capability is added to the platform itself, not to a script somebody ran once. The routing table, the ingest contract, the dataset registry, the sandbox and the scorer are all part of the product, so the next student inherits them working. That is the difference between a lab that has done an experiment and a lab that has built somewhere to do the next one.

sections.heading: Three detector families, one sealed holdout
sections.body: Every in-domain number on this sheet is the same 1,977 images, held out of training and scored the same way. Five detectors were trained on it across three families. The deployable one is the smallest that kept its accuracy, at 2.6 M parameters, and the spread between families is smaller than the spread between seeds of one family.

sections.heading: Fifteen models that were never trained on weeds
sections.body: One deterministic pass each, no repeats, on the same images. The best open vision-language model reaches a fraction of the fine-tuned detector. This is the measurement that decides where a language model belongs on this platform: judging and reviewing, not detecting.

sections.heading: What extra compute at test time buys
sections.body: The deployable checkpoint, unchanged, given more views per image. Fusing without extra views buys nothing. Multi-scale with a horizontal flip buys a little and costs three passes per frame, which a robot running at 1 Hz can afford and a laser cart cannot.

sections.heading: Which weeds it still misses
sections.body: Per-class performance of the deployable checkpoint across the twelve species. The spread between the best and worst class is larger than every training change we made this year put together, which is why the next labels matter more than the next architecture.

sections.heading: What the detector actually draws
sections.body: One checkpoint, sixteen held-out images, all twelve species. Nothing here was cherry-picked for a box: the images were drawn one per class and the model was run at the confidence the cart deploys at. Where it fires twice on one plant, or names a neighbouring species, that is on the plate too.

sections.heading: What the rover records
sections.body: A single camera frame says nothing about a robot, so this is nine, one per drive. Robot 241 streams 640 x 360 at 1 Hz alongside GPS and two IMUs, and the platform files each drive as its own dataset the moment the session opens.

sections.heading: What the cart records
sections.body: Two cameras: one forward, one down over the work zone. The platform receives laser state, vehicle telemetry and the cart's own detections with every batch. It receives no position at all, which is the gap that stops these frames becoming a map.
